english: Records where surveys were conducted but the taxon was not documented.
The degree to which the model matches the reality of a taxon's distribution.
A set of mathematical rules that can be followed to produce an outcome.
The degree to which a model is suitable for a given application, including model assumptions, performance, and insights.
Statements taken as true without proof, often used to simplify complex systems or make predictions.
The probability that a random species presence and a random species absence are correctly ordered by the classifier; AUC values above 0.75 are considered potentially useful.
A set of locations, often unsampled, used to characterize predictors across the study area and contrast with locations where the focal taxon has been detected. Also known as pseudo-absence data.
The primary units for bird population management in North America.
A prediction with two outcomes, typically positive and negative. Binary predictions are often produced by thresholding a continuous prediction of probability.
The minimum rectangular area of a given object or data extent (e.g., raster or vector layer).

An ensemble modelling technique that builds a series of small decision trees sequentially ("boosting"), with each new tree correcting the errors of the previous ones to improve overall predictive performance.
Any model or method with a binary or categorical outcome (e.g. presence-absence).
The numerical value that quantifies the strength and direction of the relationship between a predictor variable and a response variable.
Predicting a species to be present at location where it is in fact absent (i.e., a false positive).
Types of materials that modelers can upload.
Environmental variables that are used to predict the likelihood of a species' distribution. Also known as predictors.
A model evaluation technique that partitions data into multiple training and testing subsets to assess how well a predictive model generalizes to independent data.
Preparation of data to ensure it is accurate, complete, and consistent before modeling. This process addresses issues like missing values, outliers, incorrect data entry, and duplicated records.
The process of including data from multiple sources or formats into a single statistical framework to enable comprehensive analysis and interpretation.

The process of dividing a dataset into separate subsets, typically for training, validation, and testing, to build and evaluate predictive models without overfitting. Methods range from non-spatial partitioning range from non-spatial (e.g., random k-fold, jacknife) to spatial partitioning (i.e., based on geographic regions, to account for spatial autocorrelation or regional differences).
A set of materials deployed by the modeler for evaluation, sharing the same use case, modeling settings.
The probability of observing a species during a survey, given it is present.
The combination of multiple individual models to create a more accurate and robust model.
Model evaluation using data-driven tests of model performance, typically by comparing independent data to model predictions.

A person using the evaluator component of the sdmEvaluationTool to review and provide feedback on a species distribution model. An evaluator can provide feedback from many valuable perspectives, including taxonomic or sampling expertise, statistical or modelling expertise, or model application for resource management.
Model evaluation using specialist knowledge to judge the model's ecological realism and applicability.
The process of making predictions beyond the range of the data set used to train the model.
A negative instance that is classified as a positive (e.g., an absence labelled as an occurrence). Also known as a commission error.
A positive instance that is classified as a negative (e.g., an occurrence labelled as an absence). Also known as an omission error.
The taxonomic group that the species modelled are all included in (e.g., birds, vertebrates, vascular plants).
A flexible type of regression that fits smooth curves to data instead of straight lines, allowing it to capture complex, non-linear relationships between variables.

Georeferencing errors occur when a map or image is not accurately aligned with real-world coordinates through inaccurate coordinate recording, incorrect coordinate entry, misinterpretations of scales/units, and using inappropriate transformation methods.
A free Microsoft cloud platform for storing, sharing, and collaboratively developing computer code.
A type of regression that relates a response variable to predictors through a link function, allowing it to handle different kinds of data such as counts, proportions, or continuous values.
The degree to which environmental conditions can support viable populations.
A proposed explanation for the relationship between a species' distribution and its environment.
Materials used to build a species distribution model, including tabular data for model training and raster layers of predictors for model prediction.
Multivariate SDMs that model multiple species concurrently to account for species interactions.

A measure of model performance that quantifies how well a species distribution model's predictions agree with observed occurrences, correcting for chance agreement, with values closer to 1 indicating stronger agreement.
A model of a species' potential distribution fit by finding probability pattern of environmental conditions with maximum entropy, given known occurrence data and environmental constraints.
The descriptive details about a species distribution model that provide context, including model design, development, and implementation.
A simplified representation of an ecological system, often mathematical, used to understand complex systems and predict outcomes.
The combination of predictions or parameter estimates from multiple models to account for model uncertainty and produce more robust, reliable results.
Systematic difference between the true value of a statistic and the estimate.
The degree of intricacy and number of parameters within a model, interactions between variables, and the complexity of the statistical method used to fit the model.
The process of assessing how well a model's predictions match reality. Model evaluation can be empirical or expert.
The process of fitting a model (i.e., model parameter estimation), optimizing the model through tuning and validation, and post-processing the model for interpretation.

The process of understanding how environmental variables influence predicted species distributions, what ecological insights the model reveals, and how those insights relate to the intended model application.
Model inputs, outputs, and metadata.
The degree to which a model's predictions align with ecological understanding and observed patterns.
The degree to which a model's accuracy is consistent across different conditions and applications.
The process of selecting the best model from a set of candidate models, typically in terms of model fit and parsimony.
Parameters that control the model training process and that are selected by the modeller before model training.
The process of optimizing a model's settings or parameters to improve its predictive performance.
Users who design, develop, implement, test and report on SDMs. Modelers provide model materials for evaluation using the sdmEvalautionTool.
List of models available for evaluation.
A collection of R code, typically a single Shiny app within a single Github repository, that provides specific functionality for the sdmEvaluationTool.
A model that predicts the occurrence of a species across multiple ecological or behavioral states.
When predictor variables in a model are highly correlated with each other, making it difficult to separate their individual effects on the response.

topic: Northern Ontario Bird Modeling Working Group (NOBMWG)
english: An ECCC-led group of modelers, bird specialists, and managers drawn from federal and provincial governments, academia and environmental non-government organizations that work together to coordinate and enhance the extraction of information from emerging bird datasets and to tailor methods, results communications, and products to the needs of relevant sectors, with focus on Northern Ontario.
Presence of a given species at a given site. Occurrence datasets can include both presences and absences.
Materials output from a species distribution model, including raster layers of predictions and uncertainty and tabular results of the model and empirical model evaluation.
Quantitative measures used to assess how well a model's predictions match observed data via empirical model evaluation.
The proportion of positive identifications that were actually correct.
A spatial map of the models' estimated probability of occurrence, occupancy, habitat suitability, relative abundance, or density.
Biotic and abiotic variables used to explain and predict species distributions. Also known as covariates.
Data consisting only of occurrences without information on surveyed absences, typically used with background points for model training.
Data consisting of both occurrences and surveyed absences.
An ensemble learning method that builds many decision trees from random subsets of data and predictors, then combines their results to improve prediction accuracy and reduce overfitting.
The proportion of actual positives that were correctly identified by the model.
The adjustment of a dataset, typically by removing data points, to create a more balanced or representative sample for model training.
A measure of model performance that quantifies the average difference between predicted and observed values, giving more weight to larger errors.
A graph of true positive rate against the false positive rate across different threshold values to show how well a model distinguishes between presence and absence.
The size of the data sample used to train and validate the model.
Systematic variation in the sites that have been sampled, which can lead to bias in environmental predictors.
An interactive R Shiny tool that integrates Modules to enable evaluation of SDMs and synthesis of expert evaluation with quantitative evaluation to inform model improvement and application.
A model that relates species occurrence or abundance data to environmental variables to make spatially explicit predictions of species distribution, habitat, or density.
A model of the observed distribution of a species as a function of the environmental predictors.
A model of the environmental conditions under which a species can exist based on information about the species' physiology and ecology.
The proportion of actual presences correctly predicted by the model, indicating how well it detects true positives. See also recall.
The tendency for nearby locations to have more similar values than distant ones, which can violate the statistical assumption of independent observations.
The process of combining information from multiple sources or datasets while accounting for differences in data types to create a more comprehensive and consistent basis for analysis or modelling.
The planned strategy for how, where, and when data are collected to ensure they accurately represent the population or area of interest.
The geographic area over which data are collected or a model's predictions are applied.
The size of the smallest unit or grid cell of data collection and model prediction.
A resampling approach that reduces clustered occurrence records by removing nearby points to minimize spatial autocorrelation and sampling bias in model training data.
The proportion of actual absences correctly predicted by the model, indicating how well it avoids false positives.
The defined geographic area used to train and predict a species' potential habitat. See also spatial extent.
The time period over which data are collected or a model's predictions are applied.
The size of the smallest unit of time used for data collection and model prediction.
An independent set of observations used to evaluate final model performance after all training and tuning are complete.
A cutoff value used to convert continuous model predictions, such as habitat suitability probabilities, into binary presence-absence outcomes.
NOBMWG members capable of using R Shiny, R, and GitHub to modify or add to the tool code.
The ability of a model built in one area or time period to accurately predict the species' distribution in a different area, different time period, or under different conditions.
Rescaling applied to predictor rasters to resolve all layers to a common spatial resolution and extent.
The degree of variability in model predictions arising from data limitations, model structure, or parameter estimation.
The process of decreasing the spatial resolution of predictions or input data to a coarser scale, typically to align with broader spatial analyses or reduce computational complexity.
All people who use the sdmEvaluation Tool, including evaluators, modelers, and tool maintainers.
A subset of observations used during model development to tune parameters and assess performance before final model evaluation.
